prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my sole preferred part and I now hold it more firmly than in round 1, because the exchange answered the reservations I had left open. It is a single invention with a concrete before and after: a magic-wavelength lattice cancels Doppler and recoil shifts while many atoms are interrogated at once, taking fractional uncertainty from the 1e-16 regime to about 1e-18, and the result is reproduced in strontium, ytterbium and mercury in independent laboratories. The two names map onto distinct and decisive contributions, Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for record accuracy, coherence and many-body-enhanced operation. On the chair's first question I find the distinction from earlier prizes real: 2005 honoured the frequency comb as a counting tool and 2012 honoured control of single quantum systems, whereas neither covers trapping and interrogating thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength. I would word the citation on the lattice clock itself and say nothing about the SI second.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation is attribution outside the two names. Early lattice-clock proposals and the work at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo, and the ytterbium and mercury clocks, are not covered, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the 2005 recognition. I judge the pairing still captures the decisive credit, but that is a judgment and not a fact, and the citation must say it is for the invention and its realisation at extreme accuracy, not for optical clocks in general. The timing argument about the pending redefinition of the second cuts both ways and I give it no weight. A further point against my own preference runs the other way: I ranked aberration correction (B009) first at the opening, and I must not let that loyalty either inflate or depress it. I have not changed my preferred configuration from round 1; what changed is that I no longer regard the overlap with 2005 and 2012 as open, after Lindroth's and Kroll's arguments, and I do not support a two-part prize.

responses.point: Kroll accepts B009 as a genuine, mature invention but ranks the lattice clock above it because it changes the limit on a fundamental measured quantity, and says he finds no combination stronger than the clock alone.
responses.response: I accept your distinction and, on reflection, it is the main reason I no longer press the corrector as a lead. Frequency is a quantity on which physics itself is tested, while the corrector improves a tool whose payoff is largely realised in materials science and chemistry, a field boundary that is a real risk for a physics prize. I also agree that the Krivanek STEM work leaves an attribution gap that the Rose, Haider and Urban trio does not close. That is why I would not propose a two-part prize pairing the clock with B009: it would add a contested allocation to an uncontested one. Your own disclosed proximity to Hall's laboratory and to laser stabilisation seems to me a reason to note it, not to discount your technical judgment.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that Hall and Hansch gave the frequency measurement tool and Wineland the control of single ions, and neither includes neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength, so the clock is a new invention and not a refinement. She also asks that the citation not be widened to timekeeping in general.
responses.response: This is the argument that settled the overlap question for me, and it is stronger coming from the atomic-structure side, since you can verify that the magic-wavelength condition and the systematic budget are sound. I would go one step further on the citation: because Katori's proposal, the first demonstrations and Ye's accuracy work are all inside the invention, the wording 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock' covers the credit without enumerating the other groups. I disagree only mildly with your suggestion that the committee need not say anything about those groups; I would keep a short note in the committee's scientific background that NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others contributed, so the allocation is not read as complete.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers trapped-ion quantum logic (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt), calling it an original, thirty-year, widely confirmed line from proposal to realisation, but concedes the experimental share is contestable and names B008 as the more compact and less disputed prize if that is not resolved.
responses.response: I take the Cirac-Zoller proposal seriously as a conceptual advance, which is why I list B022 as an alternative. Your own concession decides it for me: the first entangling gates came substantially from NIST and Innsbruck, Wineland's 2012 prize covers the foundation, and choosing Blatt over Monroe is a judgment call. Your observation that the lattice clock also builds on 2005 and 2012 is fair, but the difference is one of degree. The clock's neighbours honoured ingredients, whereas B022's experimental neighbour is the very platform on which the gates were first shown. I would revisit B022 if the committee settled the experimental allocation, but that is not settled here.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, accepting that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and that Cao and other experimentalists lie outside the three names, and argues a prize can precede mechanism.
responses.response: I accept that a prize can precede a settled mechanism, and I do not hold the debate about the superconductivity against the discovery. My difficulty is the credit: the decisive 2018 experiments were done largely by Cao and collaborators, and with Fatemi, Dean and Young as parallel claims, a three-name set built on the prediction and the group leader is the weaker part. I think a narrowly worded citation on flat bands and correlated phases is possible, but it would be a stronger prize once the experimental credit is clearer. I am not saying never; I am saying it is a better candidate in a later year than the clock is now.

uncertainties: Whether other lattice-clock groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo, ytterbium and mercury clocks) have a claim the two names omit; I cannot verify their relative weight from the supplied files.
Whether a citation limited to the lattice clock will be seen as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, given Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work.
For B009, the allocation between Rose, Haider and Urban and the independent STEM corrector work of Krivanek is recalled from memory and unverified.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second affects the timing; I treat it as neutral.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure from round 1 stands. I am a transmission electron microscopist and so field-adjacent to B009 (Rose, Haider, Urban); I should be treated as non-neutral on that candidate and would recuse from a final decision on it if it became a leading part. My profile documents no personal collaboration with the credited individuals. For B008, the lattice clock, and for B022, no specific conflict is apparent from my profile. Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers, but his stated alternatives do not involve me.
